lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Cerberus — we're kin, after all, me being a dog myself — tell me by the Styx, what was Socrates like when he came down to you? Figured you, being a god, could do more than just bark; you can speak like a human when you want to.

lines.speaker: Cerberus
lines.text: From way off, Menippus, he looked like he was coming in with a completely steady face. Didn't seem scared of death in the slightest, and he wanted to show that to the people standing outside the mouth. But once he ducked inside the chasm and saw the darkness, I gave him a nip on the foot with the hemlock and dragged him down — and then he started wailing like a baby and crying for his own children, changing his tune every which way.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: So the man was a sophist after all, and didn't really despise the whole business?

lines.speaker: Cerberus
lines.text: No, but since he saw it was inevitable, he put on a bold front as if he was facing it willingly — the thing he had to go through anyway — so the onlookers would be impressed. And I could say the same about all of them: brave and bold right up to the entrance, but once they're in, it's a thorough exposure.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: And how did I seem to you when I came down?

lines.speaker: Cerberus
lines.text: You alone, Menippus — and Diogenes before you — did it the way your kind should. No one forced you or shoved you in; you came in willingly, laughing, and told everyone else to wail.
